prompt: A batch that runs every five minutes, all day, starts how many jobs a day?

choices.text: It already did part of the work and must know which part
choices.why: Right. Start too early and something is done twice; too late and something is skipped.

choices.text: Kafka deletes the input of a processor that crashed

choices.text: A stream cannot be restarted without rebuilding the cluster
choices.why: Restarting a consumer is ordinary; the question is where it resumes.

choices.text: The batch's input was smaller
choices.why: Size is not the difference; a closed period is.

prompt: A manager asks the stream processor for "total sales". What does the course say has to be added to the question?

choices.text: A schema, so the cents are read correctly

choices.text: A second consumer group that reads the same topic
choices.why: Another reader still faces a stream with no end.

choices.text: A slice of time, because the stream never ends
choices.why: Right. Every aggregate over a stream is over a window.

choices.text: A faster broker, so the total is computed sooner
choices.why: Speed does not give an endless stream a total.

prompt: The board reads a sales report once a quarter, and nobody acts on it sooner. What serves it best?

choices.why: Keeping events is fine; reading them live adds nothing here.

choices.text: Exactly-once transactions
choices.why: A guarantee does not decide whether a stream is worth it.

prompt: A consumer has silently fallen two hours behind at 3 a.m. Which of lesson 1's "four things that change" is this about?

choices.text: Running it again is not free

choices.text: It never stops, so it must be operated

prompt: Which of these keep costing while the shops are closed and no sale is written? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The consumers, polling for what does not come

choices.text: A nightly batch job that has finished

prompt: What does raising a producer's linger.ms from 0 to 100 trade?

choices.text: A little delay for fewer, larger batches

prompt: A member of a group crashes and another member is given its partition. Where does the new member start reading it?

choices.text: Where the crashed member had read up to in memory
choices.why: That memory died with it.

prompt: When does auto.offset.reset decide where a consumer starts?

choices.why: Right. Or when the committed one no longer exists.

choices.text: After every rebalance, since the partitions changed hands
choices.why: A rebalance hands over committed positions.

choices.text: Only on topics with one partition
choices.why: It applies per partition on any topic.

choices.text: Every time the consumer starts
choices.why: A committed offset takes precedence.

prompt: Why does the cooperative-sticky strategy disturb a group less than the eager range strategy?

choices.text: It lets two members read the same partition during the change
choices.why: That would break the group's one-reader rule.

choices.text: It rebalances less often
choices.why: It rebalances on the same membership changes.

choices.text: It gives every member all partitions
choices.why: Each partition still has one reader in the group.

choices.text: It stops only the partitions that move
choices.why: Right. Eager takes everything back from everybody first.

prompt: Which of these make a consumer group rebalance? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A member crashes and its session times out

choices.text: A member commits an offset
choices.why: A commit records a position; it changes no assignment.

prompt: A producer uses acks=1 and the leader dies a moment after acknowledging. What can be lost?

choices.text: Only messages from other producers

choices.text: The partition goes offline
choices.why: The leader is still there.

choices.text: The follower becomes leader, since it is the least loaded

choices.text: They wait for it for ever
choices.why: That is what the ISR exists to avoid.

choices.text: The trigger is continuous, so no batch is ever replayed
choices.why: Continuous is at-least-once only.

choices.text: The source is replayable and the sink idempotent
choices.why: Right. A replayed batch must do no harm.

choices.text: The checkpoint is on the local disk
choices.why: Local disk is where it should not be on a cluster.

prompt: Spark's mode that reads each record as it comes, with millisecond latency and at-least-once only, is called ___ processing.
Which of the three engines needs no cluster of its own?

choices.text: Kafka Streams
choices.why: Right. It is a library inside your own program; you scale by starting copies.

choices.text: None: all three need a cluster
choices.why: Kafka Streams needs only the Kafka cluster it reads.

choices.text: Spark Structured Streaming
choices.why: It runs on a Spark cluster or a session in your job.

choices.text: Apache Flink
choices.why: Flink needs a JobManager and TaskManagers.

prompt: A Flink job's code changes and it must be upgraded without losing its counts. What is the habit lesson 13 recommends?

choices.text: Kill it and let the next checkpoint restore it
choices.why: Checkpoints are Flink's own, for failures, and may not suit a changed job.

choices.text: Replay the topic from the beginning
choices.why: Possible, but it throws the state away and costs the whole history.

choices.text: Copy the TaskManager's memory to the new cluster
choices.why: State is saved through snapshots, not memory copies.

choices.text: Stop with a savepoint, start from it
choices.why: Right. A savepoint is the snapshot you ask for and keep.

prompt: In Kafka Streams, a stream in which each record is a separate event is a ___, and a table kept from it is a KTable.
Match each engine to where it keeps its state.

pairs.right: in a state backend, snapshotted by checkpoints
in local stores, backed up to changelog topics

prompt: Results are needed in milliseconds, state is large, and there are several sources besides Kafka. Which engine does lesson 13 point to?

choices.text: A plain consumer with a dictionary
choices.why: Large state and many sources are exactly what it lacks.

choices.text: Flink
choices.why: Right. When the stream is the product.

choices.text: Kafka Streams
choices.why: It reads and writes Kafka only.

choices.text: Spark Structured Streaming in micro-batches
choices.why: A batch interval is not milliseconds.

prompt: Why does a Flink checkpoint pass a barrier through the stream instead of each operator saving state on its own timer?

choices.text: So every operator saves the same cut
choices.why: Right. Separate timers would save inconsistent pieces.

choices.text: To stop the stream while saving
choices.why: Records keep flowing; that is the point.

choices.text: Because operators have no clocks of their own to time a save
choices.why: They do; consistency is the reason.

choices.text: To write the state into Kafka
choices.why: That is Kafka Streams' changelog, not Flink's checkpoint.

prompt: Why does change data capture also catch a change made by a script somebody ran at midnight?

choices.text: PostgreSQL forwards scripts to Debezium
choices.why: It forwards nothing but WAL through the slot.

choices.text: Scripts must publish to Kafka too
choices.why: Nothing has to publish; that is the point.

choices.text: It reads the WAL
choices.why: Right. It does not matter who made the change.

choices.text: Debezium polls every table every second
choices.why: It follows the log; it does not poll tables.

prompt: Which number should a team alert on first for a Debezium connector on PostgreSQL?

choices.text: The number of tables in the publication
choices.why: It rarely changes and threatens nothing.

choices.text: The WAL retained by each replication slot
choices.why: Right. A stopped reader makes the database keep WAL until the disk fills.

choices.text: The size of the Kafka topic
choices.why: Retention bounds it; the slot is the danger.

choices.text: Connect's memory, which grows with every captured table
choices.why: Useful, but the disk is what takes the database down.

prompt: For PostgreSQL's WAL to carry whole rows for CDC, wal_level must be set to ___.
What does REPLICA IDENTITY FULL buy, and what does it cost?

choices.text: Faster snapshots, for nothing
choices.why: It does not speed snapshots, and it is not free.

choices.text: Exactly-once delivery to Kafka
choices.why: It is about what the WAL records, not delivery.

choices.text: Tombstones on deletes
choices.why: Debezium writes tombstones whatever the identity.

choices.text: The old row, for more WAL
choices.why: Right. On a wide, busy table the cost is real.

prompt: Finance wants each stock change to say which customer caused it, and the table has no such column. What does lesson 14 suggest?

choices.text: Turn on REPLICA IDENTITY FULL
choices.why: The old row still has no customer in it.

choices.text: Read the customer from source.ts_ms
choices.why: That is a time, not a customer.

choices.text: Publish a business event through an outbox
choices.why: Right. CDC events are row changes; business meaning has to be written down.

choices.text: Add every table to the publication
choices.why: More tables do not add a fact nobody recorded.

prompt: Put the journey of one committed UPDATE to a Kafka topic in order.
items: The transaction's change is written to the WAL before COMMIT returns
pgoutput decodes it for the slot's reader
Debezium, inside Kafka Connect, turns it into a change event
The event is written to the table's topic, keyed by primary key

prompt: What can a log do that a queue cannot?

choices.text: Let a new reader start from last month
choices.why: Right. A queue deleted what it delivered.

choices.text: Redeliver a message whose consumer died before acknowledging
choices.why: That is a queue's strength.

choices.text: Accept messages from many producers
choices.why: Both do.

choices.text: Deliver a message to one consumer
choices.why: Both can.

prompt: Why can a queue add a worker during the busiest hour, when a Kafka group may not gain anything from one?

choices.text: Kafka forbids adding consumers while busy
choices.why: It allows it; the extra member may simply be idle.

choices.text: Queues keep messages for longer
choices.why: They delete them on acknowledgement.

choices.text: Queues are faster than logs
choices.why: Speed is not the difference.

choices.text: Any free consumer takes the next message
choices.why: Right. Competing consumers need no partitions planned.

prompt: In SQS, what plays the part of RabbitMQ's acknowledgement?

choices.text: Closing the connection
choices.why: SQS is request-based; nothing is tied to a connection.

choices.text: Deleting the message after the work
choices.why: Right. Until then it only became invisible for the visibility timeout.

choices.text: Receiving the message
choices.why: Receiving hides it for a while; it comes back if not deleted.

choices.text: Committing an offset
choices.why: SQS has no offsets.

prompt: Each message asks for a PDF that can take two minutes. Why does lesson 15 lean towards a queue rather than a Kafka topic?

choices.text: It holds up one worker only
choices.why: Right. A Kafka consumer's progress is a position in partition order.

choices.text: Queues guarantee exactly once
choices.why: Queues are at-least-once too.

choices.text: PDFs need replay
choices.why: Replay is the log's strength, the opposite argument.

choices.text: Kafka cannot hold messages that large
choices.why: The message is a request, not the PDF.

prompt: In RabbitMQ, a queue republishes the messages it gives up on to a dead-letter ___.
SNS with one SQS queue per reader gives every reader its own copy. What does it still not give them?

choices.text: Delivery to more than one reader
choices.why: That is exactly what the fan-out gives.

choices.text: At-least-once delivery
choices.why: Each queue delivers at least once.

choices.text: The past: a queue subscribed today starts empty
choices.why: Right. Its own copy of the future, not of the past.

choices.text: Per-message acknowledgement
choices.why: SQS has it, as deletion.

prompt: A group's lag is 1200 messages. Producers write 20 a second and the consumer handles 30. How many seconds until it catches up?
Why is lag in time the number to promise on, rather than lag in messages?

choices.text: It is smaller
choices.why: Size is not the point.

choices.text: It says how stale the output is, whatever the traffic
choices.why: Right. A thousand messages is a second on one topic and hours on another.

choices.text: Kafka reports it directly
choices.why: It has to be computed from timestamps.

choices.text: It never lies
choices.why: It trusts record timestamps, which can be wrong.

prompt: A consumer's handling sometimes exceeds max.poll.interval.ms. What does the group go through?

choices.text: The broker slows the producer down
choices.why: Consumers pull; producers are never held back by them.

choices.text: The message is skipped
choices.why: Its offset was not committed, so it is read again.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as heartbeats continue
choices.why: Heartbeats keep the session, not the poll interval.

choices.text: Repeated rebalances
choices.why: Right. Every slow message costs two rebalances.

prompt: A consumer is stuck on one bad record, and its partition shows a lag of zero. How can that be?

choices.text: The consumer moved to another partition
choices.why: It is stuck where it is.

choices.text: The bad record was deleted by retention while it was stuck
choices.why: Then it would not still be stuck.

choices.text: Lag counts from commits, and it has none
choices.why: Right. A poison message can stop a consumer while lag reads zero.

choices.text: Zero lag means the consumer is healthy
choices.why: That is the trap.

prompt: A new version of a stock consumer must recompute everything while the old one keeps serving. What does lesson 16 call this, and what group does it use?

choices.text: Reprocessing, under a new group and a new output
choices.why: Right. Blue-green: switch readers when it has caught up.

choices.text: A rebalance, under both groups
choices.why: Groups do not share partitions.

choices.text: Compaction, under no group
choices.why: Compaction is a topic's cleanup.

choices.text: A replay, under the old group, moved back to the beginning
choices.why: Moving the old group back would show old numbers while it catches up.

prompt: Which of these should wake somebody at night? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An offline partition
choices.why: Yes: reads and writes to it fail now.

choices.text: Lag in time above what the output promises
choices.why: Yes: the promise is already broken.

choices.text: Free disk running low on a log volume
choices.why: Yes: a full disk stops writes and does not recover by itself.

choices.text: A lag of 1000 messages on a busy topic
choices.why: On a busy topic that may be a second.

choices.text: A consumer committing every second
choices.why: That is normal behaviour.

prompt: 200 000 messages a day, 100 bytes each on disk, kept 30 days, 3 copies. How many gigabytes? (1 GB = 1 000 000 000 bytes)
A topic is written at 1 MB/s with three replicas, and two consumer groups read all of it. How many MB/s cross the network in all: in, between brokers and out?
Why does the cost of a stream follow the clock rather than the work?

choices.text: Messages are larger at night
choices.why: Size does not change with the hour.

choices.text: Retention is counted in hours, so every hour adds to the bill
choices.why: Retention is part of the bill, not the reason it follows the clock.

choices.text: Kafka charges by the hour
choices.why: Kafka is software; the machines are what cost.

choices.text: Its machines and consumers run all day, sized for the peak
choices.why: Right. A quiet night costs what a busy noon costs.

prompt: A till sends one sale every few seconds with compression on. Why does it compress far worse than a producer that sends thousands at once?

choices.text: Compression needs acks=all
choices.why: Unrelated settings.

choices.text: Kafka compresses a batch at a time, and its batches hold one sale
choices.why: Right. There is nothing to share between messages in a batch of one.

choices.text: Slow producers fall back to a weaker codec to save processor time
choices.why: The codec is a setting, not a speed.

choices.text: The broker decompresses slow batches
choices.why: It stores what arrives in the topic's codec.

prompt: Under a managed service that bills per partition hour, what does creating 100 partitions "for later" on a quiet topic cost?

choices.text: A bill today for every partition, used or not
choices.why: Right. Lesson 3's advice to choose deliberately has a price on it.

choices.text: Only storage
choices.why: The unit here is the partition, not the byte.

choices.text: Less than 10 partitions, thanks to volume discounts
choices.why: No such rule is described.

choices.text: Nothing until traffic arrives
choices.why: Partition hours count whether busy or idle.

prompt: A topic keeps a year of events and almost nobody reads anything older than a week. What fits it?

choices.text: Compaction
choices.why: Events are not last-value-per-key state.

choices.text: A replication factor of 1
choices.why: That trades safety, not price of old data.

choices.text: Tiered storage
choices.why: Right. Long retention, rare reads of the old part, at two prices.

choices.text: Shorter segments
choices.why: Segment size changes deletion granularity, not price.
